Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 3.pdf ---
IPG Job Manager
So the thing is, right now our grid users rely on Globus GRAM 
to run their jobs on remote machines across IPG, and honestly 
it just doesn't cut it anymore. People keep asking for things 
like being able to stage several sets of files at once, run 
more than one executable as part of the same submission, and 
actually look back at what happened with a job after the fact 
— none of that is really there today. We keep hearing 
complaints that there's no good history of executions, so when 
something goes wrong nobody can tell what happened or why. 
 
What I'm picturing is a Job Manager that lets users move and 
copy files between systems and kick off applications on 
whatever machine they're authorized to use, and they should be 
able to do this either through an API or from the command 
line, whichever fits their workflow. The core idea is a job 
made up of a main sequence of steps — file operations and 
execution operations chained together reliably — and then, if 
they want, an optional cleanup part that fires afterwards to 
delete temp files and directories whether the job succeeded or 
blew up halfway through. If something fails partway through 
the main sequence, I'd expect the system to stop, run the 
cleanup tied to whatever failed plus the cleanup for 
everything that already ran, going backwards, so we don't 
leave junk scattered across machines. 
 
It also needs to play nice with how the grid already handles 
security — there's a proxy/credential thing tied into the Grid 
Security Infrastructure that has to be respected, and only 
authorized users should ever be able to touch the systems on 
the list the Job Manager manages. And whatever we build, it 
has to keep some kind of resource list so people can only 
submit to machines that are actually registered, not just 
anywhere. 
 
On the people side, we've basically got two kinds of usage. 
Regular users will connect through the client side — find a 
server, submit a job, check on it, cancel it, look up old 
runs, that sort of thing. Then there's the admin side: someone 
has to install and keep the server itself running, someone 
manages the actual hardware and OS underneath it (might be the 
same person, might not), and there's also whoever takes care 
of the software repository server. Worth keeping in mind these 
admin folks need their own way to manage who has access, 
manage that resource list, browse jobs, and have some kind of 
log of what admin actions were taken. 
 
A couple of things I want to be upfront about not worrying 
about right now. Running one application split across two 
machines at the same time with them talking to each other — 
co-scheduling, that kind of multi-machine parallel execution — 
that's interesting but not something we need for this round. 
Same with building out a full workflow/DAG language with a GUI 
to draw out job flows, staging files in parallel instead of 
one at a time, juggling file permissions across different OS 
types when staging, or any kind of file caching to speed 
things up — all of that can wait, it's not critical for what 
we need delivered now. Also heads up, this version won't be a 
drop-in replacement for whatever the old Job Manager did 
before, so we'll need to help existing users transition rather 
than assume their old scripts just keep working. 
 
One more practical thing: whatever we ship needs to actually 
tell people when something breaks — a real error name, a 
message, and ideally the reason behind it, plus a way to log 
errors to a file users can point to themselves. And it should 
have some sense of timeouts so things don't just hang forever 
waiting on a response. 
 
One more thing since this is federal software built for NASA's 
IPG program, the whole thing has to meet Section 508 
accessibility requirements, not just some corner of it, so 
that's not something we can skip just because most of our 
users are pretty technical.

Sistema: IPG Job Manager

Resumo executivo: The IPG Job Manager enables authorized grid users to define, submit, monitor, cancel and review jobs executed on registered remote resources. It supports file movement, file copying, multiple executable steps, ordered job execution, optional cleanup actions, API and command-line access, execution history, error diagnostics and administrative control. The system improves traceability, operational reliability and resource governance within NASA's IPG environment.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - Grid user (Usuário primário): Discover registered servers, submit jobs, monitor execution, cancel jobs, inspect execution history and diagnose failures.
  STK-02 - Job Manager server administrator (Usuário primário): Install, operate and administer the Job Manager server, users, resources, jobs and administrative audit records.
  STK-03 - Resource and operating-system administrator (Usuário secundário): Maintain the hardware and operating systems represented in the managed resource list.
  STK-04 - Software repository administrator (Usuário secundário): Maintain the software repository server used by the IPG environment.
  STK-05 - NASA IPG program (Stakeholder externo): Obtain a governed, traceable and Section 508-compliant job-management capability for the IPG program.
  STK-06 - Grid Security Infrastructure (Stakeholder externo): Provide and validate proxy credentials used to authenticate grid users.
  STK-07 - Managed IPG resource (Stakeholder externo): Receive authorized file operations and application execution requests.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Authorized access to managed resources: Only users authorized for a resource may perform operations on that resource.
  RN-002 - Grid credential requirement: A user must present a valid Grid Security Infrastructure proxy credential to access grid resources.
  RN-003 - Ordered main job sequence: The main portion of a job consists of ordered file-operation and execution-operation steps.
  RN-004 - Failure handling and cleanup order: When a main-sequence step fails, subsequent main-sequence steps must not execute and applicable cleanup actions must execute in reverse order, including cleanup associated with the failed step.
  RN-005 - Administrative accountability: Administrative actions must be attributable to the administrator who performed them.

    6. The system executes the main sequence in order.
    7. The system records the final status.
  UC-002 - Monitor and cancel a job | Ator: Grid user

    3. The actor requests cancellation when the job is eligible.
    4. The system marks the job cancelled.

    1. The actor submits history-query parameters.
    2. The system searches execution records.
    3. The system displays matching records with status and diagnostics.

    1. The actor selects user-access or resource-list administration.
    2. The actor submits a configuration change.
    3. The system validates the change.
    4. The system stores the change.
    5. The system records the administrative action.
  UC-005 - Handle an execution failure | Ator: Grid user
    1. A main-sequence operation fails.
    2. The system stops subsequent main-sequence operations.
    3. The system executes applicable cleanup operations in reverse order.
    4. The system records the error name, message and available cause.

Glossário:
  IPG: NASA's Information Power Grid program environment.
  Job: A submitted unit composed of an ordered main sequence of file and execution operations, with optional cleanup operations.
  Main sequence: The ordered set of primary operations that constitute the main execution of a job.
  Cleanup operation: An optional operation associated with a job step to remove temporary files or directories after execution.
  Grid Security Infrastructure: The grid security environment responsible for proxy credentials and identity validation.
  Proxy credential: A delegated credential used by a grid user to authenticate operations on remote resources.
  Registered resource: A remote machine recorded in the Job Manager resource list as an eligible target.
  Execution history: Persistent records describing previous job submissions, statuses, operations and diagnostic results.
  Co-scheduling: Coordinated simultaneous execution of one application across multiple machines.
  DAG: Directed acyclic graph used to represent workflow dependencies.
  Section 508: United States federal accessibility requirement applicable to electronic and information technology.

Base: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 §9.6 · IEEE 830-1998 §3 · Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o 
que o sistema deve fazer e sob quais condições de qualidade. Ele serve de referência para 
desenvolvedores, testadores, gerentes e clientes durante todo o ciclo de vida do projeto.
1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem 
quando o requisito está concluído.
• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.
1.2 Como os Artefatos se Interconectam
Os artefatos formam uma cadeia de rastreabilidade. Cada RF deve ter origem em um STK 
(stakeholder) ou RN. Cada HU deve ter pelo menos um RF associado. Cada RF e HU devem ter pelo menos um CA. Esta rastreabilidade garante que nada seja implementado sem justificativa de 
negócio e que tudo que foi prometido seja testável.
Cadeia de rastreabilidade mínima:
STK → (RN →) RF → HU → CA

IPG Job Manager
So the thing is, right now our grid users rely on Globus GRAM 
to run their jobs on remote machines across IPG, and honestly 
it just doesn't cut it anymore. People keep asking for things 
like being able to stage several sets of files at once, run 
more than one executable as part of the same submission, and 
actually look back at what happened with a job after the fact 
— none of that is really there today. We keep hearing 
complaints that there's no good history of executions, so when 
something goes wrong nobody can tell what happened or why. 
What I'm picturing is a Job Manager that lets users move and 
copy files between systems and kick off applications on 
whatever machine they're authorized to use, and they should be 
able to do this either through an API or from the command 
line, whichever fits their workflow. The core idea is a job 
made up of a main sequence of steps — file operations and 
execution operations chained together reliably — and then, if 
they want, an optional cleanup part that fires afterwards to 
delete temp files and directories whether the job succeeded or 
blew up halfway through. If something fails partway through 
the main sequence, I'd expect the system to stop, run the 
cleanup tied to whatever failed plus the cleanup for 
everything that already ran, going backwards, so we don't 
leave junk scattered across machines. 
It also needs to play nice with how the grid already handles 
security — there's a proxy/credential thing tied into the Grid 
Security Infrastructure that has to be respected, and only 
authorized users should ever be able to touch the systems on 
the list the Job Manager manages. And whatever we build, it 
has to keep some kind of resource list so people can only 
submit to machines that are actually registered, not just 
anywhere. 
On the people side, we've basically got two kinds of usage. 
Regular users will connect through the client side — find a 
server, submit a job, check on it, cancel it, look up old 
runs, that sort of thing. Then there's the admin side: someone 
has to install and keep the server itself running, someone manages the actual hardware and OS underneath it (might be the 
same person, might not), and there's also whoever takes care 
of the software repository server. Worth keeping in mind these 
admin folks need their own way to manage who has access, 
manage that resource list, browse jobs, and have some kind of 
log of what admin actions were taken. 
A couple of things I want to be upfront about not worrying 
about right now. Running one application split across two 
machines at the same time with them talking to each other — 
co-scheduling, that kind of multi-machine parallel execution — 
that's interesting but not something we need for this round. 
Same with building out a full workflow/DAG language with a GUI 
to draw out job flows, staging files in parallel instead of 
one at a time, juggling file permissions across different OS 
types when staging, or any kind of file caching to speed 
things up — all of that can wait, it's not critical for what 
we need delivered now. Also heads up, this version won't be a 
drop-in replacement for whatever the old Job Manager did 
before, so we'll need to help existing users transition rather 
than assume their old scripts just keep working. 
One more practical thing: whatever we ship needs to actually 
tell people when something breaks — a real error name, a 
message, and ideally the reason behind it, plus a way to log 
errors to a file users can point to themselves.

Expected challenges
The presence of an existing system leads to common challenges that both enhancement and 
replacement projects will face, including the following:
■ The changes made could degrade the performance to which users are accustomed.
■ Little or no requirements documentation might be available for the existing system.
■ Users who are familiar with how the system works today might not like the changes they are 
about to encounter.
■ You might unknowingly break or omit functionality that is vital to some stakeholder group.
■ Stakeholders might take this opportunity to request new functionality that seems like a good 
idea but isn’t really needed to meet the business objectives.
Even if there is existing documentation, it might not prove useful. For enhancement projects, 
the documentation might not be up to date. If the documentation doesn’t match the existing 
application’s reality, it is of limited use. For replacement systems, you also need to be wary of carrying 
forward all of the requirements, because some of the old functionality probably should not be 
migrated.
One of the major issues in replacement projects is validating that the reasons for the replacement 
are sound. There need to be justifiable business objectives for the change. When existing systems 
are being completely replaced, organizational processes might also have to change, which makes it 
harder for people to accept a new system. The change in business processes, change in the software 
system, and learning curve of a new system can disrupt current operations.

2 BACKGROUND
This section briefly describes ISO 29148 emphasizing the suggested process items with which 
the axes of analysis are established and presents the relevant aspects of RE and the UC 
paradigm.
2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148
ISO 29148 is a systems and software engineering standard that specifies the required 
processes to determine the product requirements (including services) of systems and software 
throughout the life cycle (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018), (IEEE-CS, 2014). ISO 29148 is aligned with 
ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 standard for software life cycle processes and ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 
standard for system life cycle processes (IEEE-CS, 2014). ISO 29148, in its first edition (2011), 
replaced the IEEE 830-1998, IEEE 1233-1998 and IEEE 1362-1998 standards, also related to 
requirements engineering (IEEE SA, 2011), becoming the main standard in RE by providing a 
model adaptable to different organizations (Selvyanti & Bandung, 2017). In 2018, the second 
edition was published, due to the need to adopt a framework oriented towards a more detailed C2-4
technical approach (Ward et al., 2018), and in Boyarchuk et al. (2020) the importance of having 
a structured process in RE to build a good software product is highlighted.
ISO 29148 establishes (ISO/IEC/IEEE, 2018): (i) a set of 3 main processes that are iteratively 
and recursively applied in the system and software life cycle (see Fig. 1); (ii) a set of 2 related 
technical processes; (iii) each main process is composed of activities with established 
objectives to achieve a correct identification and good description of requirements; (iv) a set of 4 
types of documents for requirements specification at business, stakeholder, system and 
software levels; (v) the concept of operations and System operational concept; and, (vi) 
guidelines to manage the evolution of requirements.
2.2 User-Centered Software Requirements
The user-centered software development approach (UCD), was stablished as a response to 
existing software development schemes, which in practical terms can be noted, were focused 
on the technical aspect of the software and associated hardware (De Bellis & Haapala, 1995), 
(Norman & Draper, 1987). The UCD gained some relevance with the publication of ISO 
13407:1999 Human-centred Design Processes for Interactive Systems (Juárez-Ramírez, 2017)
and after that, when the stakeholders are included into ISO 9241-210:2010 Ergonomics of 
human-system interaction - Part 210: Human-centred Design for Interactive Systems (Vidal et 
al., 2012). Finally, the latest edition of the ISO 9241-210 standard is, recently, from 2019 (IEEE 
SA, 2011). In short, as pointed out by several authors (Juárez-Ramírez, 2017), (Forbrig, 2016), 
(Nieva et al., 2016), (Wanderley et al., 2014), and the ISO 13407 standard itself (ISO, 2019), 
RE should allow to reach an understanding of the needs, attitudes, motivations and behaviors of 
users that are the basis for achieving successful products and services, with a wide margin of 
end-user satisfaction.

É Stakeholder ou Ator?
Stakeholder = quem tem interesse no sistema (pode não usá-lo diretamente).
Ator (Caso de Uso) = quem INTERAGE diretamente com o sistema.
Todo Ator é Stakeholder; nem todo Stakeholder é Ator.
É Premissa ou Restrição?
Premissa = fato ASSUMIDO como verdadeiro sem confirmação formal. Pode mudar.
Restrição = limite IMPOSTO que não pode ser negociado (lei, orçamento, prazo, tech).
É escopo IN ou OUT?
IN = funcionalidade que o SISTEMA DO PROJETO vai implementar.
OUT = funcionalidade que fica em outro sistema ou versão futura.
Regra prática: se está em outro sistema já existente → OUT.PARTE 4 — Armadilhas Comuns na Extração Automática

3.2.4 Cenários e storyboards (L3)
Os cenários de uso descrevem, na forma de um exemplo realista, como um usuário 
interagirá com o sistema proposto [RoCa2002].
Um storyboard é um cenário visualizado. Ele se parece com uma história em quadrinhos,

ou produto deve ser usado. A reflexão sobre um exemplo concreto permite que clientes e 
usuários visualizem os requisitos na situação real do aplicativo e, assim, os revisem e alterem 
[RiFl2014].
3.3 Ferramentas de pensamento (L2)
As técnicas de elicitação apresentadas até agora representam técnicas que descrevem 
uma determinada maneira de coletar informações ou produzir um determinado produto de 
trabalho para fins de elicitação de requisitos.
Nesta seção, são apresentadas técnicas que cruzam esses tipos de técnicas, pois 
promovem uma determinada maneira de pensar. Nós as chamamos de técnicas de apoio e 
ferramentas de pensamento, porque elas não são aplicadas sozinhas, mas em conjunto com 
outras técnicas.
3.3.1 Pensamento em níveis de abstração (L2)
Os níveis de abstração são uma poderosa ferramenta de raciocínio na elicitação de 
requisitos [GoWo2005], [Laue2014]. Eles costumam ser usados como um tipo de modelo de 
processo para estruturar o trabalho de elicitação, ou seja, primeiro elicite os requisitos 
apenas no nível mais alto e continue com os níveis seguintes. Além disso, pode ser usado 
para estruturar as informações de requisitos obtidas, para identificar lacunas nos requisitos 
ou requisitos desnecessários e para concentrar as atividades de elicitação em um 
determinado nível de abstração. Por exemplo, em um workshop com usuários, é 
aconselhável concentrar-se no contexto do sistema, pois os usuários são os especialistas no 
contexto do sistema. Falar sobre as estruturas de dados de um sistema pode não ser 
apropriado, pois os usuários não se importam com as estruturas de dados internas.

2.8 Critérios de Aceite (CA)
Base: BABOK® v3 §10.1 — 'Acceptance and Evaluation Criteria'; Wiegers & Beatty (2013, cap. 10); North (2006) —

Então o sistema deve enviar e-mail de confirmação ao cliente em até 60 segundos.PARTE 3 — Heurísticas Rápidas de Classificação
Quando um trecho de texto é ambíguo, aplicar estas perguntas diagnósticas:
É RN ou RF?
Pergunta: 'Esta regra existiria sem software?' SIM → RN. NÃO → RF.
Pergunta: 'Menciona tela, botão, banco de dados ou API?' SIM → RF.
Pergunta: 'É uma política de negócio de uma área?' SIM → RN.
É RF ou RNF?
Pergunta: 'Descreve uma AÇÃO do sistema?' SIM → RF.
Pergunta: 'Descreve uma QUALIDADE/PROPRIEDADE do sistema?' SIM → RNF.
Teste: 'O sistema deve [verbo]...' → RF. 'O sistema deve ter [atributo]...' → RNF.
É HU ou RF?
HU = perspectiva do USUÁRIO, linguagem de negócio, descreve NECESSIDADE.
RF = perspectiva do SISTEMA, linguagem técnica, descreve COMPORTAMENTO.
Uma HU geralmente gera 1 ou mais RFs detalhados.
É Stakeholder ou Ator?
Stakeholder = quem tem interesse no sistema (pode não usá-lo diretamente).
Ator (Caso de Uso) = quem INTERAGE diretamente com o sistema.
Todo Ator é Stakeholder; nem todo Stakeholder é Ator.
É Premissa ou Restrição?
Premissa = fato ASSUMIDO como verdadeiro sem confirmação formal. Pode mudar.
Restrição = limite IMPOSTO que não pode ser negociado (lei, orçamento, prazo, tech).
É escopo IN ou OUT?
IN = funcionalidade que o SISTEMA DO PROJETO vai implementar.
OUT = funcionalidade que fica em outro sistema ou versão futura.
Regra prática: se está em outro sistema já existente → OUT.PARTE 4 — Armadilhas Comuns na Extração Automática
Requisito fantasma (Gold Plating)
O documento menciona uma funcionalidade que ninguém pediu explicitamente — foi adicionada 
por quem escreveu o documento como 'boa ideia'. Sinal: funcionalidade descrita sem stakeholder 
associado e sem ligação a um objetivo de negócio.
AÇÃO: extrair como HU/RF com prioridade 'Could have' e sinalizar para validação.
Dois requisitos em uma frase ('e')
'O sistema deve cadastrar e consultar clientes.' → dois RFs distintos.
'O sistema deve ser rápido e seguro.' → dois RNFs distintos.
AÇÃO: sempre separar em IDs distintos quando há 'e' ligando funcionalidades.
Requisito negativo mal formulado
'O sistema não deve perder dados.' → Impreciso. O que é 'perder dados'?

Elicitação de Requisitos | Syllabus | ©IREB 33 | 43
Um conflito de requisitos pode ser interpretado como um tipo especial de conflito social e é 
definido da seguinte forma: "Um conflito na Engenharia de Requisitos (conflito de requisitos) 
é uma incompatibilidade de requisitos, com base em uma percepção contraditória de dois 
ou mais stakeholders." [RueA2014]. Há vários indicadores pelos quais os conflitos podem ser 
detectados. Os indicadores podem ser observados na comunicação e na documentação.
Os indicadores comumente encontrados na comunicação são:
▪ Negação
▪ Indiferença
▪ Pedantismo
▪ Questões de detalhes
▪ Interpretação incorreta
▪ Ocultação
▪ Delegação
Os indicadores comumente encontrados na documentação são:
▪ Declarações contraditórias dos stakeholders
▪ Resultados conflitantes da análise de documentos ou sistemas
▪ Requisitos inconsistentes em detalhes
▪ Uso inconsistente de termos na especificação
A maioria dos conflitos tende a ser oculta e só pode ser detectada por meio do 
monitoramento cuidadoso desses indicadores. Se um dos indicadores ocorrer, isso não 
significa que haja um conflito de requisitos. No entanto, o Engenheiro de Requisitos deve 
estar sempre atento. Na maioria das atividades de elicitação de requisitos, ele estimula os 
stakeholders a exporem suas posições com clareza, revelando, em alguns casos, problemas 
inesperados ou conflitos existentes.
4.2 Análise de conflitos (L3)
Uma vez identificado um conflito, o Engenheiro de Requisitos deve esclarecer se o conflito 
identificado é ou não um conflito de requisitos. Essa distinção é importante, pois a resolução 
de um conflito de requisitos é a principal responsabilidade do Engenheiro de Requisitos, 
enquanto outros conflitos devem ser resolvidos por outros participantes (p. ex., um gerente 
de projeto).
A análise das características de um conflito de requisitos ajuda o Engenheiro de Requisitos a 
entender sua natureza. As seguintes características [RueA2014] de um conflito podem 
ajudar a entender sua natureza e a encontrar uma solução adequada:
▪ Tipo de conflito
▪ Assunto do conflito
▪ Requisitos afetados
▪ Stakeholders envolvidos
▪ Opiniões das diversos stakeholders

Os requisitos também podem ser organizados em estruturas de documentação além dos 
documentos clássicos.
Os documentos mais utilizados são:
▪ Especificação de Requisitos dos Stakeholders
▪ Especificação dos Requisitos de Usuários (um subconjunto de uma especificação 
dos requisitos dos stakeholders, abrangendo apenas os requisitos dos usuários)
▪ Especificação dos Requisitos de Sistema
▪ Especificação de Requisitos de Negócio
▪ Documento de Visão
Estruturas alternativas de documentação frequentemente utilizadas:
▪ Backlog do produto
▪ Backlog da sprint
▪ Mapa de histórias
Tanto a seleção de uma estrutura de documentação como a organização interna da 
estrutura escolhida dependem de:
▪ O processo de desenvolvimento escolhido (5)
▪ O tipo de desenvolvimento e domínio
▪ O contrato (um cliente pode prescrever o uso de uma determinada estrutura de 
documentação)
▪ O tamanho do documento
Os templates de documentos podem ajudar a estruturar uma especificação de requisitos. 
Os templates estão disponíveis na literatura [Vole2020], [RoRo2012] e em normas 
[ISO29148]. Os templates também podem ser reutilizados de projetos anteriores, similares 
ou podem ser impostos por um cliente. Uma organização também pode decidir criar um 
template como um padrão interno.
3.7 Protótipos na Engenharia de Requisitos (L1)
Na ER, os protótipos são um meio de especificar os requisitos através do exemplo e de 
validar os requisitos. Em particular, os protótipos podem ser usados se os stakeholders não 
quiserem escrever e revisar produtos de trabalho baseados em linguagem natural ou em 
modelos.
Os protótipos exploratórios [LiSZ1994] são usados para criar um entendimento comum, 
esclarecer requisitos ou validar requisitos em diferentes níveis de fidelidade. Eles são 
descartados após o uso.
▪ Wireframes são protótipos de baixa fidelidade construídos com materiais simples ou 
ferramentas de esboço que servem principalmente para discutir e validar ideias de 
design e conceitos de interface com o usuário.

5)
O escopo define com precisão o que será feito (IN) e o que NÃO será feito (OUT). A lista OUT é tão 
importante quanto a lista IN — ela previne o scope creep, que é a principal causa de projetos 
atrasados e acima do orçamento.
ESCOPO — Estrutura
Nome do sistema: [Nome]
Descrição em uma frase: [O sistema X permite que Y faça Z.]
EM ESCOPO (IN):
 • [Funcionalidade / módulo A]
 • [Funcionalidade / módulo B]
FORA DE ESCOPO (OUT):
 • [Funcionalidade excluída A] — Motivo: [justificativa]
 • [Funcionalidade excluída B] — Motivo: [justificativa]
PREMISSAS:
 • PA-01: [Fato assumido como verdadeiro — se mudar, gera risco]
RESTRIÇÕES:
 • REST-01: [Limitação tecnológica, regulatória, de prazo ou orçamento]
EXEMPLO — Sistema de Gestão de Pedidos
Nome: Sistema de Gestão de Pedidos (SGP)
Descrição: O SGP permite que vendedores registrem pedidos, acompanhem status e gerem relatórios de 
vendas via interface web.
EM ESCOPO (IN):
 • Cadastro e gerenciamento de clientes
 • Registro e acompanhamento de pedidos
 • Geração de relatórios de vendas
 • Notificação por e-mail ao cliente
FORA DE ESCOPO (OUT):
 • Módulo de contabilidade fiscal — responsabilidade do sistema ERP existente • Aplicativo mobile — previsto para v2.0
PREMISSAS:
 • PA-01: O cliente já possui infraestrutura de e-mail SMTP configurada.
RESTRIÇÕES:
 • REST-01 (Tecnológica): Banco de dados obrigatoriamente PostgreSQL 14+ (infraestrutura existente).
 • REST-02 (Regulatória): Conformidade com LGPD (Lei 13.709/2018).
 • REST-03 (Prazo): MVP entregue em 90 dias.
2.2 Stakeholders e Perfis de Usuário
Base: BABOK® v3 §2 — 'Stakeholder Engagement'; Sommerville (2016, cap. 4)
Stakeholders são todas as partes com interesse no sistema: usuários diretos, gerentes, 
patrocinadores, equipes de suporte, auditores e sistemas externos. Identificar todos os 
stakeholders no início evita requisitos descobertos tarde no projeto.
STAKEHOLDER — Estrutura por entrada
ID: STK-NN
Nome / Papel: [nome ou papel genérico]
Tipo: Usuário primário | Usuário secundário | Stakeholder externo
Nível de acesso ao sistema: Total | Parcial | Nenhum
Principais necessidades: [o que este perfil precisa que o sistema faça 
por ele]
EXEMPLO — Stakeholders do SGP
STK-01 | Administrador do sistema | Usuário primário | Total
 Necessidades: configurar permissões, cadastrar usuários, auditar logs.
STK-02 | Vendedor | Usuário primário | Parcial
 Necessidades: registrar pedidos, consultar histórico de clientes, emitir orçamentos.
STK-03 | Cliente final | Usuário secundário | Nenhum (recebe notificações)

GABARITO — Project Scenario 3: IPG Job Manager
Use: "ground_truth" field for RAGAS (context_precision / context_recall).
Each line is an atomic, checkable claim against the scenario text and the
knowledge base — not a full SRS, just the set of facts a well-grounded SRS
for this scenario should be able to cover.

- Users can move/copy files between systems and launch applications on authorized machines, via API or command line.
- A job consists of a main sequence of file and execution operations, executed reliably in order.
- An optional cleanup step can run after the main sequence, whether the job succeeded or failed.
- On failure partway through the main sequence, the system must run cleanup for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
- The system must integrate with the existing Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism.
- Only authorized users can access the systems the Job Manager manages.
- The system must maintain a resource list; users can only submit jobs to registered machines.
- Regular users interact through a client: find a server, submit a job, check on it, cancel it, look up old runs.
- Admin roles include: server installer/maintainer, hardware/OS manager, and software repository server manager.
- Admins need their own way to manage access, manage the resource list, browse jobs, and view a log of admin actions.
- Co-scheduling (running one application split across two machines simultaneously) is explicitly out of scope for this version.
- A full workflow/DAG language with a GUI is explicitly out of scope for this version.
- Parallel file staging, cross-OS file permission handling during staging, and file caching are explicitly out of scope for this version.
- This version is not a drop-in replacement for the old Job Manager; existing users need transition support.
- Error reporting must include a real error name, a message, and ideally the reason, plus file-based error logging.
- The system must implement timeouts so operations don't hang forever waiting on a response.
- As federal software built for NASA's IPG program, the whole system must meet Section 508 accessibility requirements.

em_escopo: Moving and copying files between systems
Launching applications on authorized machines, via API or command line
A job composed of a main sequence of file and execution operations, executed reliably and in order
Optional cleanup step after the main sequence, on both success and failure
Reverse-order cleanup on partial failure of the main sequence
Integration with the Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism
Resource list (registered machines) and restriction of submission to those machines
Client for regular users (find server, submit, check, cancel, look up history)
Administrative functionality (manage access, manage resource list, browse jobs, admin action log)
Structured error reporting (name, message, reason) and file-based error logging
Timeouts to prevent operations from hanging indefinitely
fora_de_escopo: Co-scheduling (running one application split across two machines simultaneously)
A full workflow/DAG language with a GUI
Cross-OS file permission handling during staging
A drop-in replacement for the old Job Manager — existing users need transition support
premissas: PA-01: The GSI (Grid Security Infrastructure) already exists and is available for integration.
PA-02: [INFERRED] Regular users have enough technical familiarity to use the API or command line.
restricoes: REST-01 (Regulatory): As federal software built for NASA's IPG program, the whole system must meet Section 508 accessibility requirements.
REST-02 (Scope): This version is not a drop-in replacement for the old Job Manager.

stakeholders.descricao: Regular user (grid user) — connects through the client to submit, check, cancel jobs, and look up old runs.
Server installer/maintainer (admin) — installs and keeps the Job Manager server running.
Hardware/OS manager (admin) — manages the underlying hardware and operating system.
Software repository server manager (admin) — manages the software repository.

regras_de_negocio.descricao: A job consists of a main sequence of file and execution operations, executed reliably and in order.
An optional cleanup step can run after the main sequence, regardless of success or failure.
On partial failure of the main sequence, cleanup must run for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
Users can only submit jobs to machines registered in the resource list.
Only authorized users (via GSI credential) can access the systems managed by the Job Manager.
This version is not a drop-in replacement for the old Job Manager — existing users need transition support, with no guarantee that old scripts keep working.

requisitos_funcionais.descricao: The system must allow users to move/copy files between systems.
The system must allow users to launch applications on machines they are authorized to use.
The system must allow these operations to be performed via API or via command line.
The system must execute a job's main sequence of file and execution operations reliably and in order.
The system must support an optional cleanup step that runs after the main sequence, on either job success or failure.
The system must, on partial failure of the main sequence, run cleanup for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
The system must integrate with the existing Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism.
The system must maintain a resource list of registered machines.
The system must restrict job submission to machines registered in the resource list.
The system must allow regular users to find an available server.
The system must allow regular users to submit a job.
The system must allow regular users to check the status of a submitted job.
The system must allow regular users to cancel a job.
The system must allow regular users to look up old job runs.
The system must allow admins to manage user access.
The system must allow admins to manage the resource list.
The system must allow admins to browse existing jobs.
The system must maintain a log of administrative actions taken.
The system must report errors with a real error name and a message, and ideally the reason.
The system must log errors to a file that the user can consult themselves.

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: System operations must implement timeouts, so they don't hang indefinitely waiting for a response.

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: The system must fully respect the Grid Security Infrastructure (GSI) proxy/credential mechanism to authorize access to managed resources.
requisitos_nao_funcionais.metrica_aceitacao: 100% of accesses to managed systems validated via GSI credential

requisitos_nao_funcionais.descricao: As federal software built for NASA's IPG program, the whole system — not just part of it — must meet Section 508 accessibility requirements.
Errors reported by the system must include a real error name, a message, and ideally the reason, and must be logged to a file accessible to the user.
requisitos_nao_funcionais.metrica_aceitacao: 100% of reported errors include a name and message; file-based log available to the user

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a regular user, I want to move/copy files between systems and launch applications on authorized machines via API or command line, so that I can run my jobs in whatever way fits my workflow.
As a regular user, I want to submit a job with a main sequence and an optional cleanup step, so that temporary files are removed regardless of whether the job succeeds or fails.
As a regular user, I want to check, cancel, and look up old runs of my jobs, so that I can manage and audit my own work.
As a server installer/maintainer, I want to install and keep the server running, so that the Job Manager stays available.
As an admin, I want to manage user access and the resource list, so that only authorized users submit jobs to registered machines.
As an admin, I want to browse existing jobs and see a log of administrative actions, so that I can monitor usage and my own team's actions.
As a user, I want to receive clear error messages (name, message, reason) and have errors logged to a file, so that I can diagnose failures myself.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Submit and run job — a user submits a job (main sequence of file/execution operations), the system executes it reliably and runs cleanup afterward (success or failure), including reverse-order cleanup on partial failure.
Manage job status — a user checks, cancels, or looks up the history of a submitted job.
Manage access and resources (admin) — an admin manages user access and the list of registered machines.
Review admin log — an admin browses the log of administrative actions taken on the system.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given a job that fails partway through the main sequence, when the failure occurs, then the system runs cleanup for the failed step and for all previously completed steps, in reverse order.
Given a user attempting to submit a job to an unregistered machine, when the submission is attempted, then the system rejects it.
Given an operation waiting for a response, when the timeout threshold is reached, then the system aborts the wait instead of hanging indefinitely.
Given any part of the system's interface, when it is evaluated for accessibility, then it complies with Section 508.
Given an error occurs during job execution, when it is reported, then the system provides a real error name, a message, and logs the error to a file accessible to the user.
